Setup Section:
Note, if you already went through the previous demos and have your prams samples in your environment, you do not need to do this,
but I am putting a simplified setup chunk for those that do not. 
```{r}
### 1. Setup ----
library(haven)
library(dplyr)
library(janitor)

### 2. Load data ----
prams <- read_sas("phase8_arf_2016_2021.sas7bdat")

### 3. Construct IPV variable ----
ipvv <- c("PAB6HUS", "PAB_XHUS", "PAD6HUS", "PAD_XHUS")

prams_IPV <- prams %>%
  filter(complete.cases(across(all_of(ipvv)))) %>%        # remove missing IPV rows
  filter(!if_any(all_of(ipvv), ~ . %in% c("B","T"))) %>%  # remove blank/teen-mom codes
  mutate(IPV = if_else(
    PAB6HUS == 2 | PAB_XHUS == 2 | PAD6HUS == 2 | PAD_XHUS == 2,
    2, 1
  ))

### 4. Create 1:1 sample (1000 yes / 1000 no) ----
set.seed(456)
prams11_sample <- bind_rows(
  prams_IPV %>% filter(IPV == 2) %>% slice_sample(n = 1000),
  prams_IPV %>% filter(IPV == 1) %>% slice_sample(n = 1000)
)

### 5. Create 1:3 sample (1000 yes / 3000 no) ----
set.seed(123)
prams13_sample <- bind_rows(
  prams_IPV %>% filter(IPV == 2) %>% slice_sample(n = 1000),
  prams_IPV %>% filter(IPV == 1) %>% slice_sample(n = 3000)
)

### 6. Select final variables for modeling ----
vars_needed <- c(
  "YY4_DOB","HISPANIC","MAT_RACE_PU","MAT_AGE_PU","MARRIED","INSNONE","PP_NONE",
  "MAT_DEG","MAT_WIC","STRS_ARG","STRS_BIL","BPG_DEPRS8","MH_PGDX8","PGINTENT",
  "CIG_1TRI","CIG_2TRI","CIG_3TRI","CIG_PRIOR","OTH_TERM","MM_NOMD","TYP_INJR",
  "PRE_ABUS","PRE_MHDP","KOTELCHUCK","ASK_ABUS","ASK_DPRS","STATE","NEST_YR",
  "VITAMIN","IPV"
)

vars <- vars_needed[vars_needed %in% names(prams11_sample)]

prams11f <- prams11_sample[, vars]
prams13f <- prams13_sample[, vars]

```


Section 2: Descriptive Analysis

2.1 Descriptive analysis of categorical variables, unweighted: As per https://emorytidal.netlify.app/prams, you can get counts for each of the categories for categorical variables in order to perform an unweighted descriptive analysis. We will be using a for loop in order to perform this for all of our categorical variables (minus our outcome variables)
```{r}
# Categorical variables 
categorical_vars <- c("HISPANIC", "MAT_RACE_PU", "MARRIED", "INSNONE", "PP_NONE", "MAT_DEG", "MAT_WIC", "BPG_DEPRS8", "MH_PGDX8", "PGINTENT", "MM_NOMD", "TYP_INJR", "PRE_ABUS", "PRE_MHDP", "KOTELCHUCK", "ASK_ABUS", "ASK_DPRS", "IPV")

#for loop to create a table for each categorical variable
for (var in categorical_vars) {
  cat("\n", var, "\n")
  print(table(prams_IPV[[var]], useNA = "ifany"))
}
```

2.2 Descriptive analysis for continuous variables, unweighted: For the continuous variables, we can use the summary function to get mean, median, max, quartiles. For loops : 
```{r}
continuous_vars <- c("MAT_AGE_PU", "CIG_1TRI", "CIG_2TRI", "CIG_3TRI", "CIG_PRIOR", "OTH_TERM")

for (var in continuous_vars) {
  cat("\n", var, "\n")
  print(summary(prams_IPV[[var]]))
}
```

2.3 Factoring and variable creation 
```{r}
#KOTELCHUCK is a variable that looks at adequacy of postnatal care using the Kotelchuck scale. Per our codebook, 1 = inadequate, 2 = interamediate, 3 = adequate, and 4 = adequate plus. What if we can make a new variable that uses the text values instead of numbers? This is where factor can come in. 

prams11f$KOTELCHUCK.f <- factor(
  prams11f$KOTELCHUCK, 
  levels = c(1,2,3,4),
  labels = c("inadequate", "intermediate", "adequate", "adequate plus")
)

#now let's generate a table to see how many for each Kotelchuck category there are per state in 2021

prams11f %>% 
  filter(NEST_YR == 2021) %>%
  with(., table(STATE, KOTELCHUCK.f,
                useNA = "ifany"))

#Just like we used case_when to create our outcome variable, we can use factoring and ifelse to create a binary variable 
prams11f$VITAMIN_4plus <- 
  ifelse(prams11f$VITAMIN > 2, 1, 0) #if >2 then 1, else 0

prams11f$VITAMIN_4plus.f <- factor(
  prams11f$VITAMIN_4plus,
  levels = c(0,1),
  labels = c("3x/week or less", "4x/week or more")
)

#stats for vitamin usage by state
table(prams11f$STATE, prams11f$VITAMIN_4plus.f, useNA = "ifany")
```

2.4 Table 1: Oftentimes, epidemiology studies have something called a "Table 1", which is the distribution of all predictor variables stratified 
by the (usually) binary outcome variable. This can help us visualize trends and associations before we start modeling. 

We can make a table 1 two ways, first, using dyplr the conventional way just to get the data points (good if you just need data points to put into a separate figure), or using the tableone package in R itself to create a table 1. 
```{r}
# function to summarize one variable
summ_var <- function(df, outcome, var) {
  df %>%
    mutate(
      across(all_of(c(outcome, var)), as.character)
    ) %>%
    count(!!sym(outcome), !!sym(var), name = "n") %>%
    group_by(!!sym(outcome)) %>%
    mutate(pct = round(100 * n / sum(n), 1)) %>%
    ungroup() %>%
    mutate(variable = var) %>%
    select(variable, IPV = !!sym(outcome), level = !!sym(var), n, pct)
}

# apply to all variables and bind into one table
table1_simple <- bind_rows(
  lapply(vars, function(v) summ_var(prams13f, "IPV", v))
)

table1_simple
```

Instead of a giant block of text, let's try using the package tableone in order to create a better looking table 1: 
```{r}
#needed packages
#install.packages("tableone")
library(tableone)

factorVars <- vars[sapply(prams13f[vars], is.factor)]

# Create Table 1
table1 <- CreateTableOne(
  vars = vars,
  strata = "IPV",
  data = prams13f,
  factorVars = factorVars
)

# Print with p-values
print(table1, showAllLevels = TRUE, quote = FALSE, noSpaces = TRUE, test = TRUE)
```
